source_text: Ἑξῆς βάρβαρόν φησιν ἄνωθεν εἶναι τὸ δόγμα, δηλονότι τὸν ἰουδαϊσμὸν, οὗ χριστιανισμὸς ἤρτηται. καὶ εὐγνωμόνως γε οὐκ ὀνειδίζει ἐπὶ τῇ ἀπὸ βαρβάρων ἀρχῇ τῷ λόγῳ, ἐπαινῶν ὡς ἱκανοὺς εὑρεῖν δόγματα τοὺς βαρβάρους· προστίθησι δὲ τούτοις ὅτι κρῖναι καὶ βεβαιώσασθαι καὶ ἀσκῆσαι πρὸς ἀρετὴν τὰ ὑπὸ βαρβάρων εὑρεθέντα ἀμείνονές εἰσιν Ἕλληνες. τοῦτ᾿ οὖν ἡμῖν ἐστιν ἐκ τῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ λεγομένων εἰς ἀπολογίαν περὶ τῶν ἐν χριστιανισμῷ κειμένων, ὄντων ἀληθῶν, ὅτι ἀπὸ Ἑλληνικῶν τις δογμάτων καὶ γυμνασίων ἐλθὼν ἐπὶ τὸν λόγον οὐ μόνον κρίνοι ἂν αὐτὰ ἀληθῆ ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀσκήσας κατασκευάσαι ἂν καὶ τὸ δοκοῦν ἐλλιπὲς ὡς πρὸς Ἑλληνικὴν ἀπόδειξιν ἀναπληρώσαι, κατασκευάζων τὴν χριστιανισμοῦ ἀληθότητα. λεκτέον δ᾿ ἔτι πρὸς τοῦτο ὅτι ἔστι τις οἰκεία ἀπόδειξις τοῦ λόγου, θειοτέρα παρὰ τὴν ἀπὸ διαλεκτικῆς Ἑλληνικήν. ταύτην δὲ τὴν θειοτέραν ὁ ἀπόστολος ὀνομάζει ἀπόδειξιν „πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως.“ [ὡς] „πνεύματος“ μὲν διὰ τὰς προφητείας ἱκανὰς πιστοποιῆσαι τὸν ἐντυγχάνοντα μάλιστα εἰς τὰ περὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, „δυνάμεως“ δὲ διὰ τὰς τεραστίους δυνάμεις, ἃς κατασκευαστέον γεγονέναι καὶ ἐκ πολλῶν μὲν ἄλλων καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ἴχνη δὲ αὐτῶν ἔτι σῴζεσθαι παρὰ τοῖς κατὰ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ λόγου βιοῦσι.
pass_a_gloss: Next he says the doctrine is barbarian from above, namely Judaism, to which Christianity is attached. And reasonably he does not reproach the fact that the word has a beginning from barbarians, praising barbarians for finding sufficient doctrines; but he adds to these things that Greeks are better at judging and confirming and exercising towards virtue the things found by barbarians. This then is for us from the things said by him a defense concerning the things lying in Christianity, which are true, that someone coming from Greek doctrines and exercises to the word would not only judge them to be true but also, having exercised, would construct and fill up what seems to be lacking as regards Greek proof, constructing the truth of Christianity. It must be said further concerning this that there is a certain proof of the word, more divine than the Greek proof from dialectic. The apostle calls this more divine proof a proof of 'spirit and power', as 'spirit' through the sufficient prophecies to testify to the one who intervenes especially concerning the things about Christ, and as 'power' through the tremendous powers, which must be constructed as having come to be and are still preserved from many other things and from their trace among those living according to the will of the word.

choices.why: indicating a logical or expected action

pass_b_english: Next Celsus declares that the doctrine is barbarian in its origin — by which he means Judaism, the root from which Christianity springs. He does not, however, reproach the word for having a barbarian beginning; on the contrary, he speaks reasonably and even praises barbarians for having discovered adequate doctrines. Yet he goes on to claim that Greeks are superior when it comes to judging, confirming, and practicing toward virtue those very things barbarians first found.

From his own words we can therefore construct a defense of the truths that lie within Christianity: someone who comes to the word from Greek doctrines and disciplines would not only recognize them as true but, by putting them into practice, would also build up and complete whatever appears lacking by the standards of Greek proof, thereby establishing the truth of Christianity.

Still more must be said: there exists a proper proof of the word that is more divine than the Greek proof derived from dialectic. The apostle names this higher proof a demonstration "of spirit and power" (1 Cor 2:4). It is "of spirit" because the prophecies are sufficient to bear witness to anyone who engages them, especially concerning Christ; and it is "of power" because of the tremendous mighty works, which must be affirmed as having occurred — not only on the testimony of many other sources but also because traces of them are still preserved among those who live according to the will of the word.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass B correctly identifies the implied scripture reference (1 Cor 2:4) for the quote 'spirit and power' which was present in the Greek but not explicitly cited in the source text, fulfilling the requirement to add identifications. Pass A and B are consistent with the Greek regarding the relationship between Judaism and Christianity, the comparison between Greek and barbarian doctrines, and the nature of the 'spirit and power' proof.

Pass A: 'ὑπὸ βαρβάρων εὑρεθέντα' translated as 'things found by barbarians'; 'ἐπὶ τὸν λόγον' translated as 'to the word'; 'πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως' translated as 'spirit and power'; 'προφητείας' translated as 'prophecies'; 'Χριστοῦ' translated as 'Christ'; 'λόγου' translated as 'word'; 'ἀπόστολος' translated as 'apostle'; 'βούλημα' translated as 'will'. Pass B: 'ὑπὸ βαρβάρων εὑρεθέντα' translated as 'things barbarians first found'; 'ἐπὶ τὸν λόγον' translated as 'to the word'; 'πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως' translated as 'spirit and power'; 'προφητείας' translated as 'prophecies'; 'Χριστοῦ' translated as 'Christ'; 'λόγου' translated as 'word'; 'ἀπόστολος' translated as 'apostle'; 'βούλημα' translated as 'will'.
